ev.childhood_friend.text.1: A child from next door calls you every day to play by the well.
ev.y_dare.text.1: The kids dare you to spend a night by the old tombs outside the city, where ghosts are said to walk.
ev.y_dare.text.1.rome: The kids dare you to spend a night among the tombs along the Appian Way, where the lemures - the restless dead - are said to wander.
ev.y_dare.text.1.athens: The kids dare you to spend a night among the gravestones of the Kerameikos, where Empusa with her donkey's leg is said to prowl.
ev.y_dare.text.1.egypt: The kids dare you to spend a night in an old tomb at the edge of the desert, where restless spirits are said to wander and jackals howl.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.1: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother}, and you an {g:uncle|aunt}. The baby was named after its grandfather and screams just as loudly as he does.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.1: On a stifling evening {npc} called you out to sit in the courtyard. You barely spoke, just watched the stars and listened to the crickets - and it was one of the best evenings of the year.
ev.c_pet.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought home a tortoise and named it after you. The household sees the resemblance: just as unhurried and just as stubborn.
ev.c_pet.text.1.rome: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} raised a jackdaw chick, and it learned exactly one word: "Ave!" Now it hails every guest like a general in triumph, and the guests don't know where to look.
ev.c_pet.text.1.egypt: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} lured a kitten into the house. In Egypt the cat is a sacred animal, so the house has a new master - and it sleeps in your spot.
ev.y_market_errand.text.1: For the first time you were sent to the market alone with money. You counted the change three times and even haggled down the price of onions.
ev.y_father_scar.text.1: {npc}, your father, showed you an old scar on his shoulder and told you about the campaign where he got it. The story changes a little every time, but you still listen breathlessly.
ev.y_full_sack.text.1: For the first time you lifted a full sack of grain and carried it to the storehouse without help. The grown-ups exchanged looks: a real worker is growing up.
ev.a_inheritance.text.1: The inheritance isn't divided yet, and {npc} already claims the whole of Father's orchard: "I looked after the old man while you were off who knows where." And {g=npc_sex:he|she} is not entirely wrong.
ev.a_inheritance.text.1.E03: The inheritance isn't divided yet, and {npc} already claims the whole olive grove: "I looked after the old man while you were off who knows where." And {g=npc_sex:he|she} is not entirely wrong.
ev.a_inheritance.text.1.JPN: The inheritance isn't even divided yet, and {npc} already wants the best rice field whole: "I'm the one who looked after the old man while you were off who knows where." And {g=npc_sex:he|she} has a point.
ev.a_inheritance.text.1.CHN: The inheritance isn’t divided yet, and {npc} already claims the best rice fields: “I looked after the old man while you were off who knows where.” And {g=npc_sex:he|she} is not entirely wrong.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.1: Your friend {npc} snatched a honey cake from a stall and ran off, and the vendor grabbed you by the ear instead. 'Who stole it? Talk, or we're going to your father!'
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.1: Your hoe clanks against something hard. Under the clods is a clay pot full of old silver and jewelry, dark with age. Someone buried it during a long-ago war and never came back. Across the boundary, your neighbor is watching.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.1.E03: The plow clanks against something hard. Under the clods is a clay pot full of heavy old coins, green with age. Someone buried them during a long-ago war and never came back. Across the boundary stone, your neighbor is watching.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.1: Before sowing an offering is needed so the gods will grant a harvest. The best animal you own will please them most - and cost you most.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.1.hindu: Before an important undertaking a puja is needed: a priest, flowers, coconuts, oil for the lamps, a generous gift to the temple. You could do it more modestly - but the gods, they say, see the heart.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.1.mesoamerican: Before sowing the gods must be fed: copal, feathers, or better still your own blood, drawn from a pierced earlobe. The priest is waiting.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.1.andean: Before sowing a llama must be offered - the finest, without a single dark spot. Guinea pigs and chicha might do, but will that be pleasing?
ev.f_sacrifice.text.1.african_traditiona: The diviner says the spirits need an offering before sowing: a goat, not a chicken - or the rains will pass your field by.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.1: The cloth merchant has a cloak dyed with a rare colour that merchants travel to the ends of the earth for. It costs as much as a craftsman earns in a year, but in it you'd look like someone people envy.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.1.E03: The cloth merchant has a cloak dyed with genuine Tyrian purple. It costs as much as a craftsman earns in a year, but in it you'd look like someone people envy.
ev.childhood_friend.text.2: New people have moved onto your street, and their child spends whole days standing to one side, watching you play. You can tell they want to come over but don't dare.
ev.childhood_friend.text.3: Every morning a herd is driven past your house, and a herd boy your age waves his stick at you. Today he asked you to come up the hill with him - all the way till evening.
ev.childhood_friend.text.4: By the stream a girl is building a whole city out of pebbles - streets, houses and a wall. She looks up and asks whether you'd like to build the gate.
ev.childhood_friend.text.5: A grubby boy with a fishing rod offers to show you a spot where the fish practically jump on the hook. He swears he has never shown it to anyone.
ev.childhood_friend.text.6: Children are playing hide-and-seek behind the sheds, and one of them has no partner. He runs up to you: "Will you team up with me? But you're not it, all right?"
ev.childhood_friend.text.7: A downpour drove you under an awning where another child was already sheltering. You stand shoulder to shoulder, and without a word they hand you half their flatbread.
ev.childhood_friend.text.8: The girl from the next yard whispers that she knows a secret way through the fence and will only show it to her best friend. It seems the post of best friend is still open.
ev.childhood_friend.text.9: You fell and skinned your knee, and a boy you didn't know helped you up and pressed a cool leaf to the scrape. Now he trails after you, waiting to hear what you'll say.
ev.childhood_friend.text.10: An apprentice boy your age hangs about the potter's workshop. He shapes little animals out of clay scraps and holds one out to you - a bandy-legged one.
ev.childhood_friend.text.11: At a festival you got lost in the crowd, and another lost child held your hand the whole time. You were found together, and now they wave to you across the whole square.
ev.childhood_friend.text.12: A child from the other end of the street has found a nest full of chicks and calls you to come and see. Two guards, they say, will keep off cats and bigger boys much better than one.
ev.childhood_friend.text.13: Older children took your toy, and a skinny boy came and stood beside you: "Now there are two of us." You didn't get the toy back, but he's still standing there.
ev.childhood_friend.text.14: A girl who never speaks to anyone silently put a shiny pebble down next to you and ran off. The next day - another one.
ev.childhood_friend.text.15: A boy from down the street carved a whistle out of a reed and learned three tunes on it. He says he'll make up a fourth if you'll listen.
ev.childhood_friend.text.16: Every evening the children play tag on the empty lot, and yesterday you nearly caught the fastest of them. Today he came over himself: "Race again tomorrow?"
ev.y_dare.text.2: The neighborhood kids dare you to spend a night in the empty house at the end of the street, where an unsociable old man died. They say the floorboards creak at night, though there's no one left to walk on them.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.2: A shutter banged in the wind, you bolted for the door and cracked your forehead on the lintel. In the morning the whole street came to admire your lump.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.2: You creaked the floorboards and moaned out of the dark so horribly that the brave lot burst out of the house, shoving each other in the doorway.
ev.y_dare.text.3: The kids bet you won't climb down the old dry well outside the village at night and bring up a stone from the bottom. They say something down there breathes.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.3: The rope slipped through your hands and you slid to the bottom, skinning your palms. The whole gang hauled you out - laughing all the way.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.3: You got to the well before anyone else and howled down into it. The echo came out so ghastly that everyone fled without waiting for you.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.3: You brought up a stone from the bottom, cold as ice. It was passed from hand to hand afterward, and even the older kids started treating you with respect.
ev.y_dare.text.4: They say lights are seen at night in the ruins on the hill, and whoever goes near them gets lost forever. The kids bet you can't sit there till morning.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.4: A light winked right beside you, you plunged straight down the slope and rolled into the brambles. The light, it turned out, was a firefly.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.4: You lit a tiny fire in the ruins and flapped a rag over it. When the kids saw the "lights", they vanished like dust in the wind.
ev.y_dare.text.5: Across the river there's a cave that breathes cold air at night - something old and hungry lives in it, they say. The kids bet you won't sit at its very mouth until dawn.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.5: Something rustled deep in the cave, you fled and tumbled down the rocks. It was bats; the bruises were yours.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.5: You hid inside the cave ahead of time and sighed heavily out of the dark. The echo rolled out so loud that the brave lot ran all the way to the river.
ev.y_dare.text.6: The kids dare you to go alone at midnight to the old crossroads outside town, where evil spirits are said to look for someone to follow home.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.6: Something stamped behind you, you fled blindly and landed in a ditch. The stamping, it turned out, was someone's stray animal.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.6: You got to the crossroads first and lay down in the road under a pale cloth. When the kids crept up, the "corpse" sat up - and the shrieking lasted all the way back to town.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.6: You stood at the crossroads until the first cockcrow, and not a single spirit followed you home. By morning the whole street knew.
ev.y_dare.text.7: They say a spirit lives in the old hollow tree by the road, and whoever climbs it at night never comes down. The kids bet you can't stay up there till morning.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.7: Something hooted in the hollow, you flinched, slipped off the branch and scraped your side raw on the bark. It was an owl; everyone else was laughing.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.7: You climbed into the hollow ahead of time, hooted like an eagle-owl, then called each of them by name. Nobody was left under the tree.
ev.y_dare.text.8: The kids bet you won't walk out at night to the old snag in the middle of the marsh, where will-o'-the-wisps are said to dance and lure people into the bog.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.8: You missed your step and sank to the waist in the bog. They pulled you out, but you stank of swamp for a week, and everyone discussed it.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.8: You smeared yourself with mud from head to toe and rose slowly out of the reeds right in front of them. They got home faster than you could start laughing.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.8: You reached the snag, tied your string around it and hopped back across the tussocks. In the morning everyone saw the string - and looked at you differently.
ev.y_dare.text.9: The kids egg you on to knock at night on the door of the old wise woman who lives on the edge of the village. They say she sees in the dark like a cat and turns anyone who bothers her into a toad.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.9: The door flew open at once, you leapt back, tripped over a trough and sprawled in the mud. The old woman just shook her head.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.9: While everyone stared at the door, you crept up behind and grabbed the last one by the heel. The shriek was heard at the other end of the village.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.9: You knocked three times. The old woman opened, looked you over and gave you a handful of dried berries: "Sweets for the brave." The kids gaped.
ev.y_dare.text.10: The kids bet you won't cross the river at night on the rotten footbridge, where drowned souls are said to grab the ankles of anyone careless.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.10: A plank cracked and you plunged chest-deep into cold water. You made it to the bank on your own, but your teeth chattered till morning.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.10: You ducked under the footbridge and grabbed the first daredevil by the ankle. His yell was heard on the next street.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.10: You crossed the footbridge and back without holding the rail. The planks creaked, the water was black, but now everyone knows who isn't afraid around here.
ev.y_dare.text.11: On the hill stands an abandoned shrine that no one visits anymore. The kids bet you can't spend a night there - the old masters of the place, they say, don't like visitors.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.11: In the middle of the night pebbles rattled down from the roof, you ran for it and went sprawling on the steps. Blood on your knees, laughter in the morning.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.11: You settled into a niche behind the wall and spoke out of it in a low, strange voice. The brave lot tumbled head over heels down the hill.
ev.y_dare.text.12: Beyond the field rises an ancient burial mound, and the old folk say that at night you can hear weapons clashing under the earth. The kids dare you to sit on top of it until dawn.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.12: Toward morning something clanked below, you rolled head over heels down the mound and twisted your ankle. It was a herdsman's bucket.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.12: You got to the mound early, knocked stone against stone and groaned from the grass. The kids decided the ancient warriors had woken, and they don't go near the mound anymore.
ev.y_dare.text.13: The kids bet you won't cross the whole field at night to the lone stone, where someone is said to sit after dark, and leave your belt on it.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.13: The shadow by the stone moved, you ran straight back and put your foot in a ditch. You kept your belt - and a limp for a week.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.13: You got to the stone first and wrapped yourself in a pale blanket. When the kids crept up, the "stone" stood up - and the field emptied in the blink of an eye.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.13: In the morning your belt hung on the stone, and every child around came running to see it. You acted as if it were nothing.
ev.y_dare.text.14: The kids bet you won't walk along the top of the old wall at night from one tower to the next - they say a sentry walks there who was never relieved from his watch.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.14: Halfway along you misstepped and slid down the rubble. The scrapes took two weeks to heal; the jeers took longer.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.14: You climbed the tower first, and when the kids came close you barked, "Who goes there?" There was no one left to answer.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.14: You walked the top of the wall from tower to tower and back. You didn't meet the sentry, but down below they greeted you like a hero.
ev.y_dare.text.15: Behind a blind wall there's an overgrown garden where a white figure is said to walk at night. The kids bet you can't stay there till morning.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.15: Something white swayed between the trees, you threw yourself at the wall and hung there, scraping your hands. The white thing was a forgotten sheet.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.15: You threw on the very sheet that was drying in the garden and walked slowly toward the kids. After that nobody talked about the "white figure" - they were too scared.
ev.y_dare.text.16: The kids dare you to climb down to the bottom of the ravine at night, where howling is heard even though there have been no wolves around for years, and bring back a branch.
ev.y_dare.accept.failure.16: The slope gave way under your feet and you slid to the bottom on your back, skinning your elbows. You brought back no branch - only bruises.
ev.y_dare.prank.success.16: You went down into the ravine first and howled up out of it so that the kids ran without looking back all the way home.
ev.y_dare.accept.success.16: You came back out of the ravine with a branch in your teeth and dirt in your hair. Nobody heard any howling - except those who imagined it.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.2: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother}. They let you hold the baby, and it gripped your finger so hard that everyone agreed: takes after its {g:uncle|aunt}.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.3: Word came from {npc}: a baby has been born, sturdy and loud. You're an {g:uncle|aunt} now and already planning what to teach the little one first.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.4: You came to congratulate them, and {npc} had fallen asleep sitting up with the baby in {g=npc_sex:his|her} arms. You quietly took the little one and rocked it half the night - your first duty as {g:uncle|aunt}.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.5: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother} and suddenly speaks in a different voice - quiet and serious. You look and can't recognize the one you used to fight with over the last bite.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.6: The house with the new baby smells of milk and hearth smoke. {npc} shows you the little one as proudly as if {g=npc_sex:he|she} had invented it, and you, the brand-new {g:uncle|aunt}, don't argue.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.7: {npc} asked you to choose a name for the baby. You thought about it for three days, and they named it their own way anyway - but the thanks were heartfelt.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.8: You brought the newborn a little charm. {npc} hung it over the cradle, and the baby stares at it for hours. Being an {g:uncle|aunt}, it turns out, is rather nice.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.9: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother}. The baby is bald, red and furious with the whole world, but somehow you think it looks like you. You're an {g:uncle|aunt} now - and that, it turns out, is a title.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.10: In the night {npc} knocked at your door, at a loss: the baby won't stop crying. You came, rocked it, hummed an old lullaby - and the child fell asleep. Since then you're the first one that house sends for.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.11: At the feast for the baby, {npc} lifted the little one over {g=npc_sex:his|her} head to show the guests. You stood closest and beamed as if it were your doing.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.12: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother}, and the whole house tiptoes now. You dropped by, sneezed loudly - and learned how fast a new parent can run.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.13: You leaned over the cradle, and the baby smiled for the very first time - at you. {npc} insists it meant nothing, but you know better.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.14: {npc} brought the baby round to show you. You held it awkwardly, like a pot of hot porridge, and it gazed at you long and gravely - as if memorizing you.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.15: {npc} has become a {g=npc_sex:father|mother}, and you, who can't make anything, spent half a day carving a rattle for the baby. It came out crooked, but the little one chews it with obvious pleasure.
ev.a_sibling_baby.text.16: When the baby was born, {npc} first cried and then laughed. You hugged {g=npc_sex:him|her} and suddenly realized you've both grown up. Now you're an {g:uncle|aunt}.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.2: {npc} woke you in the night: "Hear that? Rain." You lay in the dark listening to the water drum on the roof, and nothing worried you until morning.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.3: After a long day {npc} sat down beside you at the dying hearth without a word and rested {g=npc_sex:his|her} head on your shoulder. The embers crackled, and you wanted neither words nor sleep.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.4: {npc} led you up the rise behind the house to watch for shooting stars. You counted seven and made a wish on each. You'll never tell anyone yours.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.5: The moon was full, and {npc} asked you to go for a walk. You went down to the river and back, chattering about nothing like in your first year - and came home just before dawn.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.6: You couldn't sleep that night, and neither could {npc}. You whispered about how you first met and laughed so hard you had to clap your hands over your mouths.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.7: {npc} brought out two cups of something hot, and you sat on the doorstep looking into the dark. Somewhere dogs barked, somewhere people sang, and where you were it was quiet and good.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.8: Late in the evening {npc} brought out some hidden sweets, and the two of you ate them by a single lamp like conspirators. A simple pleasure - yet you remember it better than many a feast.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.9: The wind swept the clouds away and the sky spilled over with stars. {npc} showed you a constellation {g=npc_sex:he|she} has called by {g=npc_sex:his|her} own name since childhood and told you a tale about it you had never heard.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.10: The night was so warm that {npc} dragged a mat out into the yard, and you slept under the open sky like when you were young. Toward morning you were woken by the dew - and by {g=npc_sex:his|her} quiet laughter.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.11: Fireflies lit up over the grass, and {npc}, like a child, caught them in cupped hands to show you. You sat out until midnight and went back in smiling.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.12: {npc} couldn't sleep for worrying, so you told silly stories until {g=npc_sex:he|she} laughed - and then dozed off on your shoulder.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.13: The storm passed and the air turned as fresh as in childhood. {npc} flung the door open, and you stood on the threshold a long while, breathing in the smell of wet earth.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.14: {npc} was mending an old basket by lamplight, and you sat beside {g=npc_sex:him|her} handing over the withies. Hardly a word was said, but it was an uncommonly cozy evening.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.15: On the way home {npc} suddenly stopped in the middle of the dark street: "Look up." The sky was such that you stood there until you were both chilled through.
ev.a_spouse_stars.text.16: Before dawn {npc} woke you to see the sunrise. You grumbled, wrapped up in a blanket, but then you watched the sky grow light in silence - and the grumbling went away.
ev.c_mischief.text.4: {npc} dressed the neighbor's dog in your best headband and paraded it down the street "visiting". The dog bore it with dignity. You never did find the headband.
ev.c_mischief.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} spent half the day digging a hole in the middle of the yard: "I want to dig through to the other side of the world." And dug through - to the pot you had buried there for a rainy day.
ev.c_mischief.text.6: {npc} decided to help around the house and washed every pot - in a puddle. There was so much pride on that little face that you couldn't bring yourself to scold.
ev.c_mischief.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} let the neighbors' ducks out "for a walk". The whole street chased ducks till dark, and {npc} directed the search.
ev.c_mischief.text.8: {npc} smeared {g=npc_sex:his|her} face with soot and spent the whole evening jumping out at passers-by from around the corner. They were very obliging about being scared - especially the old neighbor, who clutched his heart for quite a while.
ev.c_mischief.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} secretly ate all the honey in the pantry and solemnly declared it was the ants. Judging by the sticky cheeks, the ants were rather small for their age.
ev.c_mischief.text.10: {npc} cut {g=npc_sex:his|her} own hair with your knife - "to look grown-up". It looks neither grown-up nor childish, but extremely determined.
ev.c_mischief.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} hid in the laundry basket and fell asleep there. Half the street searched all afternoon, and the missing child turned up on its own - by the snoring.
ev.c_mischief.text.12: {npc} brought home a stray dog and announced it was a guest. The guest ate your supper, lay down on your bed and left only in the morning, with a polite yawn.
ev.c_mischief.text.13: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} climbed onto the shed roof and refused to come down without a promise of a honey cake. The negotiations were long: {npc} got the cake, and you got your first grey hair.
ev.c_mischief.text.14: {npc} spent the whole day mimicking the pompous neighbor - his walk, his cough, the way he scratches his ear. It was so spot-on that you laughed till you cried, and for a long time afterward couldn't meet his eye.
ev.c_mischief.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} set up "shop" by the well, selling pebbles to passers-by at the price of nuts. Two people bought some. You don't know whether to scold or be proud.
ev.c_mischief.text.16: {npc} poured water into your shoe and moved a frog in - "it'll be cozy in there". The frog evidently agreed: in the morning it was still there.
ev.c_pet.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} picked up a puppy in the street, skinny and flea-bitten. Now the puppy sleeps by the door, eats better than anyone in the house, and {npc} never leaves its side.
ev.c_pet.text.3: {npc} carried home a frog in cupped hands and settled it in a water jar. The frog croaks all night, and {npc} insists it's just wishing everyone good night.
ev.c_pet.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} nursed a chick that had fallen out of its nest. The bird is long since grown but has no plans to leave: it lives under the roof and steals crumbs right off the table.
ev.c_pet.text.5: {npc} caught a cricket, keeps it in a little box made of bark and feeds it leaves. At night the cricket sings so loudly no one can sleep, but {npc} is delighted.
ev.c_pet.text.6: {npc} adopted a snail and named it Lightning. Every morning there's a race in the yard: Lightning versus a blade of grass. So far the grass is winning.
ev.c_pet.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} begged a duckling off the neighbors. The duckling has decided that {npc} is the most important duck in the world and waddles after {g=npc_sex:him|her} all over the yard.
ev.c_pet.text.8: {npc} brought home a lizard and built it a house out of potsherds. The lizard suns itself on the doorstep and eyes the guests so sternly that they wipe their feet.
ev.c_pet.text.9: {npc} tamed the mouse that used to steal grain from the storeroom. Now the mouse takes the grain openly, with permission - and apparently twice as much.
ev.c_pet.text.10: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought home a caterpillar in a pot and feeds it fresh leaves. {g=npc_sex:He|She} promises it will one day turn into "the most beautiful butterfly in the world". You're waiting just as eagerly.
ev.c_pet.text.11: {npc} fished a tiny fish out of the stream and gave it a home in a bowl. The fish received a name, a spot by the window and more attention than many a guest.
ev.c_pet.text.12: {npc} made friends with a crow, and the crow started bringing shiny trinkets to the door. Now it drags home everything that glitters - including, it seems, other people's things.
ev.c_pet.text.13: A stray dog has moved into the yard, and {npc} feeds it from {g=npc_sex:his|her} own bowl. The dog has grown fat and important, guards the house and barks at everyone except its small {g=npc_sex:master|mistress}.
ev.c_pet.text.14: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} found an enormous horned beetle in the garden and introduces it to guests: "This is Warrior." Warrior lives in a box and is said to have already defeated two other beetles.
ev.c_pet.text.15: {npc} brought home a wild dove with a broken leg and nursed it like a real healer. The dove recovered and now flies to the doorstep every morning - to see how things are.
ev.c_pet.text.16: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought home an owlet that had fallen from its nest. It sleeps by day, hoots by night and stares at everyone with round eyes, as if it knows something unflattering about each of you.
ev.c_question.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why the river never runs out if it's always flowing away. You started explaining about rain and mountains and by the end had confused yourself.
ev.c_question.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked whether dogs dream and whether they dream about people. You both watched the neighbor's dog twitching its paws in its sleep and decided: yes, and it's chasing them.
ev.c_question.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked what you were like when you were little. You started telling and were surprised to find you remembered far more than you thought.
ev.c_question.text.6: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why the stars don't fall on our heads. You said they're nailed firmly to the sky - and now {npc} wants to know who nailed them and with what.
ev.c_question.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked whether {g=npc_sex:he|she} would ever be older than you. On learning that no, {npc} was very upset and promised to try anyway.
ev.c_question.text.8: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked where the wind lives when it isn't blowing. You said, "It rests beyond the mountains." Next morning {npc} was packing a bundle to go and visit it.
ev.c_question.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why people speak different languages and whether you could learn them all in one summer. You didn't have the heart to disappoint and said it was worth a try.
ev.c_question.text.10: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked who the very first person was and who fed them. You began with the old legends, but {npc} was already asking who fed the ones who did the feeding.
ev.c_question.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why the moon follows {g=npc_sex:him|her} wherever {g=npc_sex:he goes|she goes}. You confessed that it follows you too, and the two of you walked about till dark, testing it.
ev.c_question.text.12: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked whether it hurts a tree when you pick its leaves. You didn't know, and {npc} spent the whole evening walking round the garden stroking the trunks - just in case.
ev.c_question.text.13: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why you can't fly, since you're grown up and can do everything. You had to admit that grown-ups can't do nearly everything. {npc} listened with deep sympathy.
ev.c_question.text.14: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked how many people there are in the world and whether they all know each other. You started counting the neighbors together, lost track at the market square and gave up.
ev.c_question.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked why you can't eat nothing but honey. You ran out of arguments before the house ran out of honey - and had to hand over a spoon.
ev.c_question.text.16: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked what would happen if you woke up before the sun. You promised to wake {g=npc_sex:him|her}, the two of you got up in the dark and watched together to see who'd be first.
ev.y_market_errand.text.2: For the first time you were trusted to sell a basket of eggs at the market. A customer tried to short-change you, but you caught it - and he paid up, embarrassed.
ev.y_market_errand.text.3: You were sent out for salt. You went round every stall, compared prices and brought home more salt than expected - and change besides.
ev.y_market_errand.text.4: The grown-ups stepped away, and you minded the stall alone for half a day. You counted the takings three times - and they tallied to the last scrap.
ev.y_market_errand.text.5: You were sent to trade a sack of grain for pots. You haggled so long and so seriously that the potter burst out laughing and threw in a little bowl for free.
ev.y_market_errand.text.6: The fishwife tried to palm off yesterday's catch on you. You sniffed, wrinkled your nose and picked a different fish - fresher and cheaper.
ev.y_market_errand.text.7: For the first time you were given the job of buying cloth at the market. You felt it and held it up to the light the way grown-ups do - and the merchant seemed to take you seriously.
ev.y_market_errand.text.8: You were sent to buy healing herbs from an old market woman. She named her price, you named yours, and you met in the middle. As you left she said, "You'll go far."
ev.y_market_errand.text.9: For the first time you took baskets woven at home to the market. You sold them all except one lopsided one - and swapped that for a handful of nuts by evening.
ev.y_market_errand.text.10: You were told to buy lamp oil. You noticed the seller's measure was crooked and quietly went to the next stall. That one poured a full measure - and winked.
ev.y_market_errand.text.11: In the market crush someone nearly robbed you, but you kept the purse in your fist the whole way. You came home with the shopping and a feeling of having grown up.
ev.y_market_errand.text.12: For the first time you were let loose in the big market alone. You bought everything you were told to, never once got lost and even haggled an extra onion.
ev.y_market_errand.text.13: For the first time you sold vegetables from the garden at the market yourself. You were so scared of your first customer that you let them go cheap, but by evening you were haggling like an old hand.
ev.y_market_errand.text.14: You were given money for a sack of flour and told sternly not to waste it. You bought the flour - and with what you saved, a handful of dried berries for everyone. Nobody scolded you.
ev.y_market_errand.text.15: At the market you traded homespun yarn for salt and crockery for the first time. It was a fair deal, and the trader said he'd expect you again next week.
ev.y_market_errand.text.16: You were sent to pay off a debt at a shop and collect an order. The shopkeeper miscounted in his own favor, you politely corrected him - and with a grunt he threw in a sweet cake for your honesty.
ev.c_pride.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has built a house of {g=npc_sex:his|her} own. At the housewarming you walked from room to room touching the walls - solid, straight - and were silently proud.
ev.c_pride.text.5: The neighbors came to thank you: your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} spent the whole night helping put out a fire on their street. You listened, and inside you everything sang.
ev.c_pride.text.6: The old master {npc} trained under said in front of everyone that the pupil has surpassed the teacher. You pretended not to hear, but remembered every word.
ev.c_pride.text.7: {npc} paid back an old loan - one you had long forgotten yourself - and with something extra. "You always taught me debts must be repaid," {npc} said with a shrug.
ev.c_pride.text.8: In a hungry spring {npc} shared {g=npc_sex:his|her} stores with neighbors who had nothing left. You heard about it from strangers - {npc} never said a word.
ev.c_pride.text.9: At a noisy gathering of neighbors {npc} spoke so sensibly that everyone fell quiet to listen. You stood in the crowd and barely stopped yourself shouting, "That one's mine!"
ev.c_pride.text.10: {npc} nursed back to health a sick neighbor the healers had given up on. Now the neighbor bows to you from afar, as if you had worked the miracle.
ev.c_pride.text.11: You watched {npc} teaching other people's children {g=npc_sex:his|her} trade - patiently, without shouting. You never managed that yourself, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} can.
ev.c_pride.text.12: A traveler from far away said he'd heard of someone called {npc} - honest and skilled. You asked him twice to make sure you'd heard right.
ev.c_pride.text.13: {npc} stood up for the weak against the strong in front of everyone and did not back down. You were frightened and proud at the same time - it turns out that's possible.
ev.c_pride.text.14: You fell ill, and {npc} sat by your bed night after night, dropping everything else. You recovered quickly - whether from the broths or from pride, who can say.
ev.c_pride.text.15: {npc} found a stranger's purse on the road and spent half a day going round the district until the owner turned up. The owner later came to tell you how well you had raised your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}.
ev.c_pride.text.16: You happened to overhear {npc} telling someone, "I learned that at home." It was about something good. You walked tall all day.
ev.y_father_scar.text.2: {npc}, your father, showed you a white scar across his palm: as a young man he grabbed a blade with his bare hand to protect a friend. He rarely tells the story, and for some reason always in a whisper.
ev.y_father_scar.text.3: Your father, {npc}, rolled up his sleeve and showed you the marks of a wild beast's teeth. "It was this big," he said, spreading his arms. Every year the beast gets a little bigger.
ev.y_father_scar.text.4: By the fire {npc}, your father, told you where the welt on his back came from: once he carried people out of a burning house. He speaks of it matter-of-factly, and you can't sleep until midnight.
ev.y_father_scar.text.5: {npc}, your father, showed you a crooked finger - a souvenir of the time he bet, as a young man, that he could shift a boulder three men couldn't. He shifted it. The finger never straightened.
ev.y_father_scar.text.6: You asked about the scar over his eyebrow, and {npc}, your father, told you about a fight with robbers on the road one night. You listened with clenched fists and breathed out with relief at the end: they drove them off.
ev.y_father_scar.text.7: {npc}, your father, showed you a scar on his knee and confessed: he fell out of a tree while stealing fruit from someone else's garden. "Not a word to anyone," he winked, and you suddenly realized your father was once small too.
ev.y_father_scar.text.8: {npc}, your father, showed you an old burn scar and told you how as a young man he worked at a firing kiln. The heat there, he says, made the very air ring.
ev.y_father_scar.text.9: By the fire {npc}, your father, showed you a long scar - an arrow wound from the war the old men don't like to talk about. He kept it short, but you remembered every word.
ev.y_father_scar.text.10: Your father {npc} showed you a mark on his shin: in a flood a log knocked him down, and he clung to a snag in the middle of the river for half a day. "The river let me go that time," he says. "But I don't trust it."
ev.y_father_scar.text.11: {npc}, your father, showed you the scar on his chin and at first said he'd fought a monster. Then he thought it over and admitted he tripped over a doorstep at someone's feast. You laughed till you got hiccups.
ev.y_father_scar.text.12: {npc}, your father, showed you a rope scar on his wrist: once on a mountain pass he slipped off the path, and a rope saved his life but tore off the skin. "I've checked every knot since," he said.
ev.y_father_scar.text.13: Your father, {npc}, sat silent by the fire a long while, then showed you a scar on his side and said, "That's for the one time I wasn't afraid." He said nothing more, which made the story all the more frightening.
ev.y_father_scar.text.14: {npc}, your father, showed you a mark on his shoulder and told you how in a hungry year he fought a wild animal over a kill. "The beast left with nothing," he grinned. "And I left with this."
ev.y_father_scar.text.15: By the fire {npc}, your father, showed you a scatter of small white scars on his arm: "Bees. I went after wild honey, and they objected." It's his funniest story - and probably his truest.
ev.y_father_scar.text.16: {npc}, your father, let you touch the deep scar on his shin and told you of a long campaign, of comrades who never came back, and of carrying a wounded man for three days. His voice shook at the end.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.3: On Christmas Eve everyone fasted until the first star. You watched for it at the window all evening and were the first to shout, "There it is!" - and then everyone ate as if they had fasted for a year.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.4: At Christmas the church was packed and hot with candles. The old woman beside you wept quietly for joy, and back then you didn't understand why - but now, perhaps, you do.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.5: On Christmas morning bread was handed out to the poor at the church, and you were trusted with a basket. You gave away the last piece and were surprised to find you didn't mind at all.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.6: At Christmas people went from house to house singing, and you went along with them. Your voice kept cracking, but everyone was treated just as generously.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.7: On Christmas night every light in the church was put out; then one candle was lit, and another from it - and soon the whole church glowed. You held your candle in both hands and were afraid to breathe.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.8: At Christmas an extra place was left at the table for any traveler who might knock. No one knocked, but you kept glancing at the door all evening.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.9: On Christmas night they read about the manger and the shepherds, and suddenly you pictured that stable so clearly it was as if you stood there yourself - in the warm breath of the animals and the smell of hay.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.10: At Christmas two neighbors who hadn't spoken for years made peace. They embraced right at the church doors, and everyone around pretended nothing special had happened.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.11: After the long fast the Christmas table seemed a miracle: meat, flatbreads, sweets. You ate so much you couldn't move until nightfall - and it was wonderful.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.12: At Christmas a little play was put on in the square: children wrapped in blankets were the Magi and the shepherds, and the neighbor's goat played the ox and the donkey at once. The goat gave the best performance.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.13: The Christmas service ended just before dawn. You stepped out of the church into the cold dark, the bell still booming overhead, and something trembled in your chest.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.14: At Christmas you gave alms from your own purse without counting. The beggar at the gate blessed you, and all through the feast you felt taller.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.15: On Christmas night everyone in the house, from the eldest to the youngest, exchanged little gifts. You got a carved wooden spoon - and you keep it to this day.
ev.f_m_christmas.text.16: No one slept the night before Christmas: there was baking, scrubbing, greenery to hang. You arrived at the service exhausted, but sang louder than anyone.
ev.y_full_sack.text.2: For the first time you dug a whole strip of field without a break. The old field hand walked along it, grunted and said nothing - which from him is the highest praise.
ev.y_full_sack.text.3: All day you hauled water from the river alongside the grown-ups and never once sat down. By evening your shoulders burned, but for the first time you were served as much food as they were.
ev.y_full_sack.text.4: At harvest you lasted a whole day from dawn to dusk for the first time. Blistered hands, a back that won't bend, and inside a pride that will last you a year.
ev.y_full_sack.text.5: You hoisted a bundle of firewood the size grown-ups carry and brought it home without once setting it down. The neighbors watched you go and shook their heads: strong.
ev.y_full_sack.text.6: A storm brought a tree down across the road, and you were called to drag it clear with the grown-ups. And you weren't just pretending to pull - everyone saw it.
ev.y_full_sack.text.7: For the first time you threshed a whole sheaf on your own, without anyone telling you how. The elders checked the straw - not a single ear missed.
ev.y_full_sack.text.8: When the dam on the stream was being repaired, you carried stones with the grown-ups and lifted the biggest one. They set it right in the foundation - your stone.
ev.y_full_sack.text.9: For the first time you carried a full basket across the ford without wetting a single grain. On the far bank one of the grown-ups clapped you on the shoulder like an equal.
ev.y_full_sack.text.10: You grubbed out an old stump nobody had managed to shift for two days. Earth flew everywhere, and you stood over the hole, out of breath and happy.
ev.y_full_sack.text.11: For the first time you brought in as much of the harvest in a day as the grown-ups. That evening you were seated not with the children but with the workers - and nobody objected.
ev.y_full_sack.text.12: For the first time you worked a whole day in the field in the rain alongside the grown-ups and didn't leave before they did. You came home soaked to the skin - and proud.
ev.y_full_sack.text.13: When the roof was being rethatched, you passed heavy bundles of straw up without a break until evening. The thatcher said that with arms like yours you could come up on the roof.
ev.y_full_sack.text.14: For the first time you ground a whole day's measure of grain on the grinding stone. Your arms are falling off, but tonight's flatbread is made from your flour.
ev.y_full_sack.text.15: You were put to digging an irrigation ditch beside the grown-ups, and by evening your stretch was no shorter than theirs. It was noticed - and the next day you were given a bigger hoe.
ev.y_full_sack.text.16: For the first time you climbed the steep path up the slope with a full basket without stopping once. At the top you turned round: the older ones were still lagging behind.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.4: Dogs barked under the windows all night - first one, then every dog in the quarter, as if debating something important. By morning they seemed to have reached an agreement. You hadn't.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.5: The craftsman next door starts hammering before daylight. You've learned to wake a moment before the first blow - from sheer anticipation.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.6: Behind the wall someone spent half the night learning to play the pipe. He never did get the tune, but you now know exactly where he goes wrong.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.7: The neighbors across the street quarreled until midnight - loudly, with banging crockery. In the morning they set off to market together hand in hand, and you never got any sleep.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.8: A baby screamed all night in the next yard, and the whole quarter stayed awake with it. In the morning everyone in the street was bleary and remarkably polite to one another.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.9: In the night a rowdy crowd went down the street, singing and banging on doors. One of the doors was yours. You never did find out what they wanted.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.10: The neighbor keeps birds on his roof, and at dawn they raise such a racket you'd think the roof was about to take off with them.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.11: The night watchmen change shifts right under your windows, calling out and rapping their clappers. After a month you started waking up on the nights they were quiet.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.12: The woman next door worked her loom all night, racing to be ready for market day. You counted the thumps like sheep, but sleep never came.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.13: In the house opposite they mourned their dead until morning - loudly, as custom demands. You lay awake thinking your own thoughts: about who will one day weep for you, and how.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.14: Two men got into a fight in the street at night, and half the neighbors leaned out of their windows to offer advice. The fight ended in a draw; the advice went on well past midnight.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.15: The baker next door fires his oven in the middle of the night, and the clatter of his peel comes with the smell of fresh bread. Both keep you awake - but at least the second is pleasant.
ev.a_neighbor_noise.text.16: The neighbors' whole clan has come in from the countryside, and now about twenty people talk at once behind the wall. You already know who owes whom and who has what temper.
ev.w_old_joints.text.3: This morning you got out of bed in three stages, groaning. Your body remembers every heavy load you ever lifted.
ev.w_old_joints.text.4: Your fingers won't bend in the mornings anymore, and you untie knots with your teeth now. The young ones snicker; you tell them to live this long first.
ev.w_old_joints.text.5: Your back seized up in the middle of the yard, and you stood there bent double until a neighbor helped you to the bench. Embarrassing - and painful.
ev.w_old_joints.text.6: Bending down for a dropped spoon has become a whole undertaking: first you consider whether it's worth it. The spoon usually wins.
ev.w_old_joints.text.7: Cold nights now ache in every joint. You put a warmed stone at your feet and remember how you once slept on bare ground without noticing a thing.
ev.w_old_joints.text.8: The road to market you once walked without a thought now needs a rest halfway. There's a handy stone there - you already think of it as yours.
ev.w_old_joints.text.9: Your shoulder aches so much you can't turn over at night. The healer woman rubs ointment into it and says, "Years can't be cured, but they can be coaxed."
ev.w_old_joints.text.10: Your knees cracked so loudly when you squatted down that the dog jumped up and barked. You explained to it that this was none of its business.
ev.w_old_joints.text.11: You couldn't get up from a low bench for a long time and finally called a neighbor's boy to help. He lifted you as easily as a sack of feathers - and that was the most galling part.
ev.w_old_joints.text.12: By evening your feet burn as if you'd walked on coals all day. You soak them in warm water with herbs and grumble at everyone who walks too fast.
ev.w_old_joints.text.13: This morning your hands were swollen and wouldn't obey, and you had to hold your cup in both palms like a child. By noon it eased - but the sting of it stayed.
ev.w_old_joints.text.14: You tripped on level ground: your foot simply didn't rise as high as you told it to. Nothing broken, but now you watch your feet like a small child.
ev.w_old_joints.text.15: You spent half a day working in the garden as if you were young again, then took two days to straighten up one piece at a time. The garden is pleased. You, less so.
ev.w_old_joints.text.16: Your neck won't turn anymore, so to see who called to you in the street you have to swing round your whole body like a boat. Your friends are used to it and call out well in advance.
ev.a_inheritance.text.2: Father has been buried, and {npc} refuses to divide the house: "I live in it and keep it up, and you have a place of your own." By law it should be split equally, but you have no wish to put your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} out on the street.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.2: The court awarded you the larger part. The house is yours now - but beyond its threshold everything feels empty.
ev.a_inheritance.text.3: Right after the funeral {npc} drove Father's herd off to {g=npc_sex:his|her} own place: "I've tended it these last years - you've never so much as laid eyes on it." And the animals really do come only to {g=npc_sex:his|her} call.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.3: The court divided the herd in your favor. You got the animals, and now your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} turns away when you meet.
ev.a_inheritance.text.4: {npc} says Father promised {g=npc_sex:him|her} the river field while he was still alive - only there are no witnesses. By law the field must be divided, and {npc} has already sown the whole of it.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.4: The court put no faith in a promise without witnesses and gave you more than half. The field is yours, and a silent grudge now stands on the boundary.
ev.a_inheritance.text.5: Father left a storehouse full of grain and goods. {npc} carted off half of it before the funeral feast: "You'd only squander it anyway - I'll keep it safe."
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.5: The court ordered the larger share returned to you. The grain came back; the family warmth did not.
ev.a_inheritance.text.6: {npc} wants Father's yard with the well - the best one for miles around: "You moved away, and I have to live off this water." And the well really does water {g=npc_sex:his|her} whole garden.
ev.a_inheritance.yield.6: Give up the yard and well
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.6: The court gave you the yard and the well. You have all the water you want now - and no one to share it with.
ev.a_inheritance.text.7: {npc} has fenced off Father's meadow beyond the village with a new wattle fence and says it was Father's dying wish. You weren't there - and there's no way to check.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.7: The court ordered the fence taken down and gave you most of the meadow. The fence came down; the wall between you did not.
ev.a_inheritance.text.8: The inheritance is a wedge of land by the woods. {npc} says, "I grubbed out every stump there while you were off who knows where." Sweat put into the soil is a hard argument to answer.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.8: The court awarded you more than half. The woodland plot is yours, and you'll dream for a long time of stumps grubbed out by other hands.
ev.a_inheritance.text.9: Father, it turns out, buried a pot of silver under the threshold. {npc} found it first and reckons that "finders are heirs".
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.9: The court divided the silver in your favor. You got the money, and your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} no longer invites you to eat.
ev.a_inheritance.text.10: {npc} wants Father's beehives: "The bees know me - they'd sting you to death." The bees seem to agree: you were stung three times yesterday.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.10: The court divided the apiary in your favor. You have the hives and the honey - and both of you have the bitterness.
ev.a_inheritance.text.11: {npc} says {g=npc_sex:he|she} rebuilt Father's hillside terraces after every downpour while you were off living your own life. "Dividing them is like dividing my back," {g=npc_sex:he|she} says.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.11: The court gave you most of the terraces. Now it's you who rebuilds them after every downpour - with no one to call for help.
ev.a_inheritance.text.12: {npc} won't let Father's pond be divided: "I dredge the silt out every year, and you only turn up to eat the fish." And {g=npc_sex:he|she} has a point.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.12: The court gave you the larger part of the pond. The fish are yours now - and so, apparently, is the silt.
ev.a_inheritance.text.13: The land was divided peacefully, but {npc} won't give up Father's belongings - the dishes, the rugs, the chests: "These are memories, not riches." Only the memories fill half a house.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.13: The court divided the goods by inventory. You carted off the chests, but the memories, it seems, stayed with your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister}.
ev.a_inheritance.text.14: {npc} claims Father's grove on the hill: "You went off to town anyway, and I've put down roots here." The trees Father planted now stand between you.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.14: The court awarded you most of the grove. The trees are yours, and their shade feels cold.
ev.a_inheritance.text.15: By law the old ancestral house, where your grandfathers lived before you, is to be shared by the two of you. {npc} says you don't slice a house like a flatbread - and wants to buy out your share for a pittance.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.15: The court valued the house fairly, and you received your full share. But in the ancestral house no one waits for you anymore.
ev.a_inheritance.text.16: {npc} has ploughed over the boundary on Father's valley land so that your half has shrunk to a third. "That's how it was in Father's day," {g=npc_sex:he|she} says. You remember it differently.
ev.a_inheritance.court.success.16: The court put the boundary back where it was and gave you an extra strip. The land is yours, and your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} now ploughs with {g=npc_sex:his|her} back to you.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.2: Your friend {npc} climbed the fence after someone else's fruit, and the orchard's owner caught you by the fence instead. "Who was it? Don't tell me, and I'm taking you to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.2: The orchard owner held on tight. Your father had to apologize and work a day in the man's orchard.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.2: You twisted free, vaulted the fence and vanished into the bushes.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.3: Your friend {npc} threw a stone, and three of the potter's pots burst apart. The potter grabbed you by the shoulder: "Who threw it? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.3: The potter didn't let go until your father came. The pots had to be paid for - all three, plus one more the potter seems to have smashed himself out of rage.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.3: You slipped out of the potter's grip and dived into the crowd.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.4: Your friend {npc} snatched a fish off the stall and was gone, and the fishwife seized you by the sleeve. "Who took it? Talk, or we're off to see your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.4: The fishwife held on tight. Your father paid for the fish, and at home you ate it in silence.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.4: You tore free, slipped on the fish scales, kept your feet and ran.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.5: Your friend {npc} opened the neighbor's bird cage - just to look - and the birds flew away. The neighbor caught you by the collar: "Whose doing was this? Don't tell me, and I'm going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.5: The neighbor didn't let go. Your father spent half a day chasing birds over the rooftops with him, then said nothing all evening.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.5: You yanked your arm free and raced round the corner while the neighbor shook his fist at the sky.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.6: Your friend {npc} swiped some hot pastries off the baker's tray and ran, and the baker grabbed you by the ear. "Who stole them? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.6: The baker was stronger than he looked. Your father had to pay for the pastries and sit through a long lecture.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.6: You left your belt in the baker's hand and vanished down an alley.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.7: Your friend {npc} untied someone's boat for fun, and the current carried it off. The boatman grabbed you by the arm: "Who untied it? Talk, or I'm taking you to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.7: The boatman held on tight. Your father spent half a day helping him chase the boat and came home soaked and furious.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.7: You twisted free and fled along the bank through the reeds.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.8: Your friend {npc} broke a comb out of someone's hive and ran, and the beekeeper caught you, covered in bees. "Who was it? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.8: The beekeeper held on until your father came running. Your father paid for the honeycomb, and you went about swollen from stings for a week.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.8: You tore free, swatting at bees, and ran without looking back all the way to the river.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.9: Your friend {npc} stuffed a shirtful of nuts from a stall and ran off, and the seller collared you. "Who was that? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.9: The seller didn't loosen his grip. Your father paid double for the nuts, and at home you didn't even get a taste.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.9: You ducked under the counter, popped out the other side - and were gone.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.10: Your friend {npc} snatched a bright ribbon off the counter and ran, and the stallholder caught you by the sleeve. "Who took it? Talk, or it's off to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.10: The stallholder held on tight. Your father had to pay for the ribbon and apologize at length in front of the whole market.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.10: You twisted loose, leaving her a scrap of your sleeve, and melted into the crowd.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.11: Your friend {npc} pulled up vegetables from the neighbor's garden, and the neighbor woman caught you by the fence. "Who was in there? Don't tell me, and I'm going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.11: The neighbor woman didn't let go. Your father worked half a day in her garden, and you worked a week.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.11: You leapt over the beds and disappeared behind the fence.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.12: Your friend {npc} lobbed a stone over a rich man's wall and hit something that shattered. A servant rushed out and grabbed you: "Who threw it? Talk, or I'm taking you to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.12: The servant held on tight. Your father had to bow at the rich man's gate and pay for the damage.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.12: You wriggled out of the servant's grip and were round the corner before he could shout.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.13: Your friend {npc} pinched a little chisel from the woodcarver - "just to look at" - and disappeared. The carver caught you by the shirt: "Who took it? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.13: The carver held on tight. Your father had to pay for the missing chisel - and gave you a long look that was worse than any scolding.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.13: You slipped out of your shirt like a snake out of its skin and ran.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.14: Your friend {npc} snatched a sweet fruit from the offerings at the shrine, and the shrine keeper caught you by the hand. "Who took it? Talk, or I'm going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.14: The keeper held on tight. Your father had to bring a new offering to the shrine - twice the size of the old one.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.14: You yanked your hand free and tumbled down the steps without looking back.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.15: Your friend {npc} pinched a clay whistle from the toymaker and started blowing it round the corner, and the toymaker grabbed you by the ear. "Who took it? Talk, or we're going to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.15: The toymaker sent for your father. He paid for the whistle and said nothing all the way home.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.15: You wriggled free and ran toward the whistling - to catch up.
ev.y_friend_caught.text.16: Your friend {npc} knocked over a jar of oil outside a shop and ran, and the shopkeeper caught you on the slippery stones. "Who broke it? Talk, or I'm taking you to your father!"
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.failure.16: The shopkeeper held on until your father came. The oil had to be paid for, and the stain on the street is still there.
ev.y_friend_caught.wriggle.success.16: You broke free and raced off, leaving oily footprints behind you.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.2: You were digging a new well when your spade struck a bundle of rotted leather. Inside are heavy silver bracelets, black with age. Someone hid them long ago and never came back. The neighbor who came to help has frozen with a basket of earth in his hands.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.2: You split the find down the middle right beside the half-dug well. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.3: The flood has gone down and undercut the bank by your field. The neck of a jar sticks out of the washed-out slope, full of silver and jewelry green with silt. Someone buried it here in some long-ago time of trouble. From the next plot your neighbor, who came out to see what the river had done, is watching you.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.3: You split the find down the middle on the wet bank before anyone else came. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.4: A storm toppled the old tree on the boundary, and something glinted among its upturned roots: a bundle of gold jewelry, netted in roots. It must have been buried under a sapling generations ago. Your neighbor came running to look at the fallen tree - and saw something else.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.5: You were taking down the old stone wall at the edge of your field, and from under the bottom stone rolled a clay pot heavy with silver. Someone hid it when the wall was built - and took the secret with them. On the other side of the wall your neighbor has just looked up.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.5: You split the find down the middle right there by the half-dismantled wall. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.title.6: The Hiding Place under the Hearth
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.6: You were rebuilding the hearth and lifted out a cracked stone, and beneath it lay a hiding place: a pouch of old silver and a pair of heavy earrings. The house's former owners never made it back for them. In the doorway stands your neighbor - come to borrow a light.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.6: You split the find down the middle right there by the torn-up hearth. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.keep.ok.6: You put the silver back in its hiding place, sealed it with the stone and spend a little at a time so nobody notices. Only the neighbor has been coming round to borrow a light suspiciously often.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.7: Looking for a stray animal, you wandered into a cave on the hillside above the fields. In a niche behind a rock is a rotted leather sack stuffed with silver ornaments. Someone hid it here from some long-ago disaster. At the entrance, panting, stands the neighbor who was searching with you.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.7: You split the find down the middle right there in the cave, by the light from the entrance. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.8: Digging a virgin patch at the edge of your field, you turned up a clod full of green-crusted bronze bowls - and in one of them, a handful of gold rings. Whose they were and from what age, no one can say anymore. The neighbor on the next strip has dropped his work and come closer.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.9: After the downpour the ground caved in among the ruins at the edge of your field. In the hole you can see a stone box, and in it silver, beads and bracelets, as if someone meant to come back for them tomorrow. Your neighbor, hearing the collapse, is already running over.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.9: You split the find down the middle right there among the ruins while no one was looking. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.10: The dog spent half the day digging by the old boundary stone and finally barked so loudly that everyone came running. In the hole is a pot of silver and jewelry, buried, it seems, back in some time of war. The owner of the next field looks from the dog to you and back.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.11: Clearing the irrigation ditch, you snagged a copper pot full of old silver with your hoe. Someone sank it in the mud long ago, meaning to come back. On the other side of the ditch stands your neighbor - and the ditch, after all, is shared.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.11: You split the find down the middle right there on the bank of the shared ditch. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.12: You were mending the floor of the old storehouse, and under a rotten plank you saw a leather sack of gold jewelry in the dirt. Whoever built the storehouse must have known - and took the secret to the grave. In the doorway stands your neighbor, come to return a borrowed hoe.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.12: You split the find down the middle right there in the storehouse with the doors shut. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.13: The rain washed away part of the slope above your garden, and the corner of a stone casket came into view. Inside are silver, beads and rings, dark with age. Your neighbor, who came to assess the storm damage, is now assessing something else entirely.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.13: You split the find down the middle right there on the washed-out slope. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.14: You reached into the hollow of the old boundary tree after wild honey, and your hand found a bundle of gold jewelry. Someone hid it there long ago and never came back. Down below, holding the ladder, stands your neighbor.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.15: You drained the old pond to clear out the silt, and something gleamed on the bottom: a pot full of silver, sunk by someone in some long-ago time of trouble. The neighbor who was helping haul the mud wiped his hands and slowly straightened up.
ev.t_buried_treasure.share.ok.15: You split the find down the middle right there on the muddy bottom of the pond. Now you have money - and someone who keeps the same secret.
ev.t_buried_treasure.text.16: The boundary stone had tilted, and your neighbor was helping you set it straight. Under it lay a hollow holding silver ingots and jewelry, hidden back in someone's great-grandfather's day. The neighbor broke the silence first: "Well, what do we do now?"
ev.f_sacrifice.text.2: You've only just recovered from a serious illness, and the priest reminds you that healing must be repaid with thanks to the gods. A generous gift is a sign of gratitude; a stingy one, of a short memory.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.3: A long journey lies ahead of you, and without an offering, they say, the road will be unlucky. What you lay on the altar is up to you.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.4: There's been no rain for two months, and the whole district is bringing gifts to the shrine. The neighbors are watching who brings what: the stingy will be blamed for every misfortune afterward.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.5: You've finished building your house, and the old folk say there will be no peace in it without an offering to the spirits of the place. Something valuable must go under the threshold - the more valuable, the sturdier the house.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.6: It's been a good year, and custom says the gods must be thanked with the best of what you have. The neighbors have already made their offerings - some generously, some just for show.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.7: For three nights running you've had the same bad dream. The diviner says the gods are displeased and names the price of their favor. It isn't small.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.8: On the day of remembrance a meal is left on the altar for those who are gone. The neighbors bring the best they have; you could bring something plainer - the dead, they say, aren't greedy.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.9: Once you made a vow: if things went well, you'd bring the gods a generous gift. Things have gone well. Then again, nobody but you heard the vow.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.10: Lightning struck the tree right beside your house. The priest says it's a sign: the gods expect a gift. And he looks at you expectantly.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.11: You're about to start a big undertaking, and those in the know advise you to win over the gods first. A generous offering, they say, pays for itself. Sometimes.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.12: A sickness is going round the district, and people are hurrying to the shrine with gifts so the trouble will pass their houses by. There's already a line at the altar, and everyone eyes what the others are carrying.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.13: The great festival has come, and the whole district is going to the shrine with gifts. The priests loudly proclaim the names of the most generous - and silently remember the stingiest.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.14: Something valuable of yours has gone missing, and the diviner promises the gods will help you find it - after an offering. The more generous the gift, he says, the surer the finding.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.15: The new year is beginning, and custom says it must be opened with an offering so that it will be kind. You stand at the altar working out what that kindness is going to cost you.
ev.f_sacrifice.text.16: You quarreled with a neighbor, and the elders say the reconciliation must be sealed with an offering to the gods. The more generous the gift, they say, the firmer the peace.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.2: The jeweler sets before you a heavy gold bracelet of fine workmanship - the kind only the grandest people wear. It costs a year of comfortable living, but your arm looks quite different in it.
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.2: The bracelet sits heavy and pleasant on your wrist. You keep adjusting it - especially when someone is watching.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.2: You handed the bracelet back. Your arm is the same as before - and seems rather more comfortable that way.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.3: The merchant shows you a belt embroidered with beads and set with silver plaques - the work of foreign craftsmen. A belt like that can be seen from far off, and so can its price.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.3: Take a similar one with copper plaques
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.3: In the new belt you stand straighter and walk more slowly - so the plaques have time to shine.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.3: You walked on. Your old belt holds up just as well - and that's all a belt is for.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.4: A merchant from a distant coast has brought a necklace of large pearls. He swears divers risked their lives for every one - and charges accordingly.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.4: Take shell beads made to look like pearls
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.4: The pearls are cool against your neck and glow softly. At the feast you catch people stealing glances at them - the best part of the evening.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.4: You said no. Let the pearls go to someone who feels incomplete without them.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.5: A master carver is selling a seat with armrests shaped like beasts, inlaid with bone and mother-of-pearl. It's no more comfortable than a bench, but guests will rise when you sit down.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.5: Take a similar one painted to look inlaid
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.5: The seat has taken the best spot in the house. You receive guests in it and feel a little like a ruler.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.5: You left the seat with the carver. Your bench is sturdy, and one can sit on it with dignity too.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.6: The merchant opens a tiny vessel, and a scent spreads that makes passers-by turn their heads. The oil was carried halfway across the world; for one vessel he asks as much as a year of good living.
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.6: Now people know you by your scent before they see you. You open the vessel a drop at a time - and only for important meetings.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.6: You left with the scent only on your sleeve. By evening it had faded - and so had the wanting.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.7: The craftsman shows you shoes of the finest leather embroidered with gold thread. Nobody walks through mud in shoes like these - they're for places where there is no mud. They cost a year's work.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.7: Take a pair stitched with copper thread
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.7: You step carefully round the puddles and catch people looking at your feet. Walking is awkward, but being looked at is lovely.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.7: You left the shoes on the counter. Your old ones at least know the way home.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.8: The merchant unrolls a length of cloth as fine as smoke and shimmering like water. They say it's woven in only one faraway land. A garment of it would cost a year's earnings.
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.8: The new garment whispers with every step. The neighbors pretend not to notice - and notice everything.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.8: You stroked the cloth goodbye and walked away. Smoke and water are no thing to wear for a year's labor.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.9: The jeweler has a ring with a stone the color of dark blood. He whispers that only one ruler ever had its like, and names the price in a whisper too - it's embarrassing to say out loud.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.9: Take one with a cheaper dyed stone
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.9: The ring flashes on your finger, and you've started gesturing more - just in passing.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.9: You shook your head. The ring brought that ruler no happiness either, they say.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.10: The merchant shows you a headdress of brilliant feathers from rare birds caught somewhere in distant forests. Wear it to a festival and everyone will notice you - and remember.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.10: Take a cheaper one with dyed feathers
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.10: At the festival all eyes were on you. The feathers swayed with every nod, and you nodded a lot.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.10: You walked on. People will notice you at the festival anyway - if you have something to say.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.11: A craftsman is selling a mirror polished to a gleam, in a carved frame. Your face shows in it as clearly as in still water - only water is free, and the mirror costs a year's earnings.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.11: Take a similar one in a cheap alloy
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.11: You hung the mirror where everyone can see it and now know your own face better than you'd like. Guests admire it - the frame and themselves.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.11: You declined. You know your own face well enough, and still water still costs nothing.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.12: The merchant shows you a casket painted in gold, with a clever hidden lock. You have nothing to keep in it, but it would stand so that every guest would ask what's inside.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.12: Take one painted to look like gold
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.12: The casket stands in pride of place. It's empty inside, but guests ask - and you smile mysteriously.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.12: You walked on. There's nothing to keep in it anyway - why pay for emptiness?
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.13: The merchant unrolls a carpet that, he says, nine weavers worked on for three years. The pattern is so fine it seems a shame to walk on, and the price is frightening.
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.13: The carpet lies in the middle of the house, and guests now take off their shoes at the door without being asked. You tread on it carefully, as if it belonged to someone else.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.13: You left the carpet with the merchant. A bare floor is more familiar - and easier on the conscience.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.14: A merchant is selling a brightly feathered foreign bird that can repeat words. Such birds are kept in palaces, and yours would be the only one in the district.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.14: Take an ordinary bird, dyed brighter
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.14: The bird has learned your name and screeches it at guests. The guests are envious; the neighbors complain.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.14: You left without the bird. Let it talk in palaces - there it'll find plenty to repeat.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.15: The jeweler shows you earrings with pendants that chime at every turn of the head. You hear them before you see them - and they cost a good craftsman's year of work.
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.15: The earrings chime every time you turn your head, and you turn it more often than necessary.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.15: You left without the earrings. The quiet around you suddenly seemed rather dignified.
ev.v_vanity_purple.text.16: The furrier shows you a cloak of rare fur, soft and dark as night. It's a bit warm to wear, but they say only the grandest people go about in one.
ev.v_vanity_purple.fake.16: Take a cheaper one of dyed fur
ev.v_vanity_purple.buy.ok.16: The fur settles softly on your shoulders. You're hot, but everyone can see you can afford it.
ev.v_vanity_purple.pass.ok.16: You walked on. The animal needed that fur more than you do.
